title: Clinical and Microbiological Outcomes of Implant-Supported Hybrid Abutment Crowns in the Posterior Region as a Function of Restorative Material – Results of a 36-Month Randomized Clinical Trial
content: Background: Hybrid abutment crowns combine a prefabricated titanium base with a custom, CAD/CAM-fabricated ceramic superstructure. Despite their increasing clinical use, only limited long-term in vivo data are currently available regarding the influence of the restoration material on clinical and microbiological outcomes. Objective: To investigate the clinical, radiographic, and microbiological outcomes of implant-supported hybrid abutment crowns in the posterior region over 36 months as a function of crown material. Materials and Methods: In a single-center, randomized, controlled clinical trial with blinded data analysis, 57 patients with single-tooth implants (Camlog iSy) in the posterior region were enrolled and, after stratification by gender and edentulous region, randomly assigned to receive restorations made of hybrid ceramic (enamic, n = 28) or lithium disilicate ceramic (IPS e.max, n = 30); 57 patients (27 HC, 30 LS2) completed the 36-month follow-up and were included in the final analysis. The primary endpoint was implant survival rate over 36 months; secondary endpoints included marginal bone resorption (ImageJ), peri-implant probing depths (Florida Probe), and the subgingival microbiome (micro-iDent plus), which were assessed at baseline and after 36 months. Results: The implant survival rate was 100%. Marginal bone resorption was generally low and stable; a statistically significant difference was observed only for gender (mesial p = 0.033), but not for jaw position, implant length, diameter, shoulder position, or crown material (p &gt; 0.05 for each). Probing depths remained low over 36 months with no clinically relevant progression; although the change in probing depth differed statistically significantly between materials (p = 0.012), this difference was not considered clinically relevant. Microbiologically, the majority of the examined bacteria showed a predominantly stable to favorable course; for individual species (including Fusobacterium nucleatum, Campylobacter rectus, Eikenella corrodens, and Capnocytophaga spp.), deteriorations occurred more frequently, particularly in the lithium disilicate group, without accompanying clinical or radiographic abnormalities. Conclusion: Implant-supported hybrid abutment crowns demonstrated high clinical and biological stability over 36 months, regardless of the restoration material used. Peri-implant tissue stability appears to be determined primarily by prosthetic design, ease of hygiene maintenance, and post-treatment care, and less so by the material class of the superstructure.
